lessons.title: Bash Scripting for DevOps: Variables, Loops, Backups and Log Checks
lessons.description: Write safe Bash scripts with variables, arguments, if tests, loops and exit codes, and build a backup script and a log summary script that were really run.

content.text: A script is a text file of commands. When you notice that you are typing the same five commands every day, that is a script waiting to be written. Scripts are the glue of DevOps: they back up folders, check that services are alive, prepare servers and run inside pipelines. Bash is the shell on almost every Linux server, so a small amount of Bash goes a long way. This lesson teaches the pieces you need and gives you three working scripts.
Why do we need it?
Servers need the same small jobs again and again: backups, checks, clean-ups. A script does them the same way every time, and can run when you are asleep. Scripts are also the glue of pipelines.
A real-life example

Writing a recipe down means anyone can cook the dish the same way. A script is a recipe for the computer. If you do not write it down, every cook does it a little differently and sometimes forgets the salt.
The first line and the safety line

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

items: `#!/usr/bin/env bash` tells the system which program should run the file.
`set -e` stops the script when a command fails, instead of carrying on and doing damage.
`set -u` treats an unset variable as an error, which catches typos.
`set -o pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if any part of it fails.

content.text: Save the file, for example as `hello.sh`, make it executable with `chmod +x hello.sh` and run it with `./hello.sh`.
Variables, arguments and quotes

NAME="devops"
echo "Hello, $NAME"
SRC="${1:?give a source folder}"      # first argument, or stop with this message
KEEP="${3:-7}"                         # third argument, default 7
TODAY=$(date +%F)                      # capture the output of a command
echo "Backup for $TODAY"

There must be no spaces around the equals sign when you set a variable. Put variables inside double quotes, as in `"$NAME"`, so that file names with spaces do not break your script. `$1`, `$2` are the arguments and `$#` is how many there are. `$?` is the exit code of the last command: 0 means success and anything else means failure.
Tests and loops

if [ -d "$SRC" ]; then
  echo "folder exists"
elif [ -f "$SRC" ]; then
  echo "it is a file"
else
  echo "not found" >&2      # send the message to the error stream
  exit 2
fi

for f in *.log; do
  echo "checking $f"
done

while read -r line; do
  echo "line: $line"
done < sample.log

items: `-d` tests for a folder, `-f` for a file, `-r` for readable, `-z` for an empty text, and `-eq`, `-lt` and `-ge` compare numbers.
Use `&&` to run the next command only if the first succeeded, and `||` to run it only if it failed.
A function groups steps: `backup() { ... }`, then call it by name.

content.text: Script 1: a backup with a retention rule

This script packs a folder into a dated `.tar.gz` and deletes the oldest backups beyond a number you choose. It was run in the course lab with four backups in a row and a limit of two, and it created four files and removed the two oldest. The script in this lesson was run on Linux in the course lab (bash 5, Python 3.13). The output shown is real. Your numbers (memory, disk, dates) will be different.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# backup.sh - tar a folder into a dated file and keep only the newest N backups.
# Usage: ./backup.sh <source_dir> <backup_dir> [keep]
set -euo pipefail
SRC="${1:?source dir}"; DEST="${2:?backup dir}"; KEEP="${3:-7}"
[ -d "$SRC" ] || { echo "no such folder: $SRC" >&2; exit 2; }
mkdir -p "$DEST"
STAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
FILE="$DEST/$(basename "$SRC")-$STAMP.tar.gz"
tar -czf "$FILE" -C "$(dirname "$SRC")" "$(basename "$SRC")"
echo "created $(basename "$FILE")"
# delete the oldest ones beyond $KEEP (names sort by date)
ls -1 "$DEST"/*.tar.gz | sort | head -n -"$KEEP" | while read -r old; do
  rm -- "$old"; echo "removed $(basename "$old")"
done

$ ./backup.sh /srv/site /srv/backups 2
created site-20261112-022321.tar.gz
created site-20261112-022322.tar.gz
created site-20261112-022323.tar.gz
removed site-20261112-022321.tar.gz
created site-20261112-022324.tar.gz
removed site-20261112-022322.tar.gz

A backup you have never restored is only a hope. After you make one, unpack it somewhere else with `tar -xzf` and check the files. Also copy backups to another machine or storage service, because a backup on the same disk does not help if the disk fails.
Script 2: summarise a log

This script counts log lines by level, shows which service has the most errors and prints the most common error messages, using `awk`, `grep`, `sort` and `uniq`. Here it runs on a small sample file. The log lines are made up.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# logwatch.sh - summarise a log file. Usage: ./logwatch.sh sample.log
set -euo pipefail
FILE="${1:?usage: logwatch.sh <logfile>}"
[ -r "$FILE" ] || { echo "cannot read $FILE" >&2; exit 2; }

echo "Lines by level:"
awk '{print $3}' "$FILE" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

echo
echo "Errors by service:"
grep ' ERROR ' "$FILE" | awk '{print $4}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

echo
echo "Most common error text:"
grep ' ERROR ' "$FILE" | sed 's/^.*ERROR [a-z]* *//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

Lines by level:
      4 INFO
      3 ERROR
      1 WARN

Errors by service:
      2 api
      1 worker

Most common error text:
      1 email failed: connection refused
      1 GET /jobs/99 500 database timeout
      1 GET /jobs/12 500 database timeout
Script 3: a health check you can reuse

This script checks that a TCP port accepts connections and that a web address answers with code 200. It exits with 0 when healthy and 1 when not, so a scheduler or pipeline can act on the result. In the lab it was tested against a small local web server: it printed OK for the home page, FAIL with 404 for a missing page, and FAIL when the server was stopped.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# healthcheck.sh - is a TCP port open, and does a URL answer 200? Exit code 0 = healthy.
# Usage: ./healthcheck.sh <host> <port> [path]
set -uo pipefail
HOST="${1:?host}"; PORT="${2:?port}"; PATH_="${3:-/}"

if ! (exec 3<>"/dev/tcp/$HOST/$PORT") 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "FAIL: $HOST:$PORT is not accepting connections"; exit 1
fi
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -m 3 -w '%{http_code}' "http://$HOST:$PORT$PATH_" || true)
if [ "$CODE" = "200" ]; then
  echo "OK: $HOST:$PORT$PATH_ answered 200"; exit 0
fi
echo "FAIL: $HOST:$PORT$PATH_ answered ${CODE:-nothing}"; exit 1

$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765 /
OK: 127.0.0.1:8765/ answered 200
$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765 /missing
FAIL: 127.0.0.1:8765/missing answered 404
$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765        # server stopped
FAIL: 127.0.0.1:8765 is not accepting connections
Good habits

items: Test scripts on copies of data, not on the real thing. Run `bash -n script.sh` to check the syntax without running it, and `bash -x script.sh` to see each command as it runs.
Never put passwords in a script. Read them from the environment or a protected file.
Make scripts safe to run twice (idempotent), because schedulers and people run things again.
Write a usage line at the top, and print clear messages. Future you will not remember.

content.text: Architecture diagram
Here is the idea as a simple picture. You can use the same diagram in your own notes.

flowchart LR
  T[Trigger: cron or pipeline] --> S[Script starts]
  S --> W[Does the work]
  W --> E{Exit code}
  E -->|0| OK[Success: continue]
  E -->|not 0| F[Fail: stop and alert]
How to check it worked

items: Your scripts stop with a clear message when an argument is missing.
`bash -n` reports no syntax errors for each script.
You restored a backup into a different folder and the files match.

content.text: How companies use it
Teams use Bash for backups, health checks, deployment helpers, log clean-up and pipeline steps. Larger logic moves to Python, but Bash stays the fastest way to join Linux commands.
Common errors and how to fix them

items: **Script works by hand but not in cron.** Use full paths and set the PATH. Redirect output to a log to see errors.
**unbound variable.** A variable name is misspelled or unset. `set -u` helped you find it.
**Spaces in file names break the script.** Quote every variable: `"$FILE"`.
**Syntax error near unexpected token.** Check missing `then`, `fi` or `done`, and run `bash -n script.sh`.
**Permission denied.** `chmod +x script.sh`, and check the first line points at bash.

content.text: Best practices

items: Start with `set -euo pipefail`.
Quote variables.
Print clear messages and use exit codes.
Never put passwords in scripts.
Test on copies and make scripts safe to run twice.

content.text: Interview questions with simple answers

items: **What is a shebang?** The first line that tells the system which program runs the file, for example `#!/usr/bin/env bash`.
**What does `set -e` do?** Stops the script on the first failed command.
**How do you read the exit code?** With `$?` right after the command.
**What does `$1` mean?** The first argument passed to the script.
**How do you make a variable with a default?** `${VAR:-default}`.
**`&&` vs `||`?** `&&` runs the next command if the first succeeded. `||` runs it if the first failed.
**How do you loop over files?** `for f in *.log; do ...; done`.
**How do you debug a script?** `bash -x script.sh` shows each command as it runs.
**Why quote variables?** To stop spaces and special characters from splitting the value.
**Bash or Python?** Bash for short Linux glue, Python for larger logic and data.

content.text: Warning: Scripts that delete files, such as backup clean-up, can destroy data if a variable is empty or wrong. Test with `echo` in front of dangerous commands first and keep `set -u` on.
Practical exercises
Try each one yourself before you look at the hint. Struggling for a few minutes is how the skill sticks.

items: Write a script that greets a name given as an argument and stops with a message if none is given. Hint: `${1:?message}`.
Write a loop that prints each `.log` file and its line count. Hint: `for`, `wc -l`.
Change the backup script to keep five backups. Hint: The third argument.
Write a script that returns exit 1 if a folder does not exist. Hint: `[ -d "$DIR" ]`.
Extend the log script to print the busiest minute. Hint: `awk` and `cut`.

content.text: Mini project: Nightly maintenance script
Combine backup, log summary and a health check into one script that runs every night from cron and writes to a log. Test it by breaking each part on purpose and confirming the exit code changes.
Knowledge test
Answer the ten questions in the quiz at the end of this lesson. You pass with 60 percent. If an answer is wrong, read the explanation, then reread the part of the lesson it points to.

steps.say: A scheduler such as cron, or a pipeline step, starts the script.
The script does its work: a backup, a log check or a health check.
It finishes with an exit code. Zero means success and anything else means failure.
Tools read the code. A pipeline stops on failure, and an alert can be sent.

faqs.q: Should I learn Bash or Python for DevOps?
faqs.a: Learn both over time. Bash is best for short glue tasks on Linux. Python suits longer logic, data handling and working with cloud APIs. This course uses Bash first and Python where it helps.

faqs.q: What does set -euo pipefail do?
faqs.a: It makes the script stop on the first failing command, on an unset variable and on a failed part of a pipe. It turns silent mistakes into clear errors.

faqs.q: Why do my scripts fail in cron but work in my terminal?
faqs.a: Cron runs with a minimal environment and a short PATH. Use full paths to commands and files and redirect output to a log file to see the error.

lessons.title: Networking Basics: OSI, TCP/IP and IP Addresses
lessons.description: Understand how computers talk over a network: the OSI and TCP/IP models, IPv4 and IPv6, public and private IPs, and how a browser reaches a server.

content.text: Every cloud service, container and website you will work with depends on a network. When a deployment fails with connection refused or timed out, you need to know where to look. Networking looks like a wall of strange letters at first, but the ideas are simple, and you can learn the useful part in a few lessons. This first one gives you the map: how data travels, what the layer models mean and what an IP address is.
Why do we need it?

Every cloud service, container and website talks over a network. When a deployment cannot connect, you need to know which layer to check. Without the basics, errors like timed out or connection refused are just noise.
A real-life example

Sending a letter has layers too. You write the letter (application), put it in an envelope with an address (network), the post office picks a truck (transport and link), and the road carries it (physical). If the letter is late, you check where it stopped. Network layers let you do the same with data.
What a network is

A network is a group of devices that can send data to each other. Your phone and laptop on home Wi-Fi are on a small network. The internet is a huge number of networks joined together. Data is cut into small pieces called packets. Each packet carries the address it is going to, the address it came from and a piece of the message. The network delivers packets, often by different routes, and the receiving device puts them back in order.
The OSI model: seven layers

To keep this manageable, network engineers describe the work in layers. Each layer does one job and relies on the layer below. The OSI model has seven layers. You do not need to memorise it for daily work, but interviewers like it, and it helps you to say where a problem is.

items: **Physical:** cables, radio signals, the bits on the wire.
**Data link:** moves data between devices on the same local network, using MAC addresses (the fixed hardware address of a network card). Switches work here.
**Network:** moves packets between networks using IP addresses. Routers work here.
**Transport:** manages the conversation between two programs: TCP (reliable) or UDP (fast). Ports live here.
**Session:** keeps a conversation open.
**Presentation:** formats and encrypts the data, for example TLS.
**Application:** the protocols programs speak: HTTP, DNS, SSH, SMTP.

content.text: A useful way to remember the order is the phrase from the bottom: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away. People like silly phrases, and any phrase that helps you is fine.
The TCP/IP model: four layers
The internet itself uses a simpler model with four layers. It is the one you will see in real life.

items: **Link:** the local network (Wi-Fi, Ethernet).
**Internet:** IP addresses and routing.
**Transport:** TCP and UDP, with ports.
**Application:** HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SSH and so on.

content.text: OSI layers 5, 6 and 7 are all one Application layer in TCP/IP. In practice, when someone says layer 4 they mean transport, TCP and ports. When they say layer 7 they mean the application, for example HTTP. You will hear these terms when load balancers are described: a layer 4 load balancer looks only at addresses and ports, and a layer 7 load balancer can read the web request.
IP addresses
An IP address identifies a device on a network, like a house number in a street. There are two versions.

items: **IPv4** has four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, for example `192.168.1.25`. It has about 4.3 billion possible addresses, which are no longer enough for all devices.
**IPv6** has much longer addresses written in hexadecimal with colons, for example `2001:db8::1`. It has a gigantic number of addresses. Many networks run both at once.

content.text: Public and private IP addresses

A public IP address can be reached from the whole internet and is unique. Private addresses are for use inside a home, office or cloud network only. Many networks can reuse the same private addresses, because those addresses are never routed over the open internet. Three ranges are reserved for private use in IPv4.

Your laptop probably has a private address such as 192.168.1.25. Your router has one public address, and translates between the two, using a technique called NAT that you will meet in a later lesson. Cloud networks use private ranges too, which is why you will choose ranges like 10.0.0.0/16 when you build a network in AWS.

The addresses in these lessons, such as 192.168.1.25 and 203.0.113.10, are examples. Addresses beginning 203.0.113, 198.51.100 and 192.0.2 are reserved for documentation, so they are safe to use in examples.
What happens when you open a web page

items: Your browser asks DNS for the IP address of the site name.
It opens a TCP connection to that address on port 443 (HTTPS).
TLS starts: the browser and the server agree on keys, and the browser checks the server’s certificate.
The browser sends an HTTP request: GET this page.
The server sends back the page, and the browser shows it.

content.text: Each of these steps can fail, and each failure looks different. A wrong name gives a DNS error. A closed port or a firewall gives connection refused or a timeout. A bad certificate gives a security warning. A broken application gives an error code such as 500. When you troubleshoot, work through the steps in order, and you will find the broken one.
Architecture diagram
Here is the idea as a simple picture. You can use the same diagram in your own notes.

flowchart TD
  A[Application: HTTP, DNS, SSH] --> T[Transport: TCP or UDP and ports]
  T --> I[Internet: IP address and routing]
  I --> L[Link: Wi-Fi or Ethernet]
  L --> P[Physical signal]
How to check it worked

items: You can explain the difference between a public and a private IP.
You can name what each of the four TCP/IP layers does.
You can say which step failed if a page shows a certificate warning.

content.text: How companies use it

Engineers design cloud networks with private ranges, route traffic through gateways, and choose which ports are open. When an app cannot reach a database they walk through the layers: name, address, port, firewall, then application.
Common errors and how to fix them

items: **Connection timed out.** Packets are being dropped, often by a firewall or a wrong route. Check security rules and routes.
**Connection refused.** The machine is reachable but nothing listens on that port, or it listens only on 127.0.0.1.
**Name or service not known.** DNS cannot resolve the name. Check spelling and the DNS server.
**Two networks cannot connect.** Their private ranges overlap. Plan non-overlapping ranges before you build.
**Works by IP but not by name.** This is a DNS problem, not a connection problem.

content.text: Best practices

items: Plan private ranges before creating networks.
Troubleshoot from the bottom up, one layer at a time.
Document your address plan.
Use private addresses for internal services.
Learn the common ports by heart.

content.text: Interview questions with simple answers

items: **Name the layers of the TCP/IP model.** Link, internet, transport and application.
**At which layer do routers work?** The network layer, using IP addresses.
**What is an IP address?** A number that identifies a device on a network.
**IPv4 vs IPv6?** IPv4 has 32-bit addresses and is running out. IPv6 has 128-bit addresses and a huge space.
**What is a private IP address?** An address for internal use, such as 10.x.x.x or 192.168.x.x, not routable on the internet.
**What is a MAC address?** The hardware address of a network card, used inside a local network.
**What happens when you open a website?** DNS lookup, TCP connection, TLS handshake, HTTP request, response.
**What is a packet?** A small piece of data with source and destination addresses.
**Switch vs router?** A switch joins devices in one network. A router joins different networks.
**What is a default gateway?** The router a device uses to reach other networks.

content.text: Practical exercises
Try each one yourself before you look at the hint. Struggling for a few minutes is how the skill sticks.

items: Find your private IP and say which private range it belongs to. Hint: `hostname -I`.
Write the five steps of opening a web page and the layer of each. Hint: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP, response.
Check which route your machine uses to reach the internet. Hint: `ip route`.
Explain public vs private IP to a friend with a street example. Hint: House number inside an estate vs the estate address.
List three problems that show up as timeouts. Hint: Firewall, route, host down.

content.text: Mini project: Home network map
Draw your home or office network: devices, private addresses, the router and the public address. Mark where NAT happens and which layer each device works at.
Knowledge test
Answer the ten questions in the quiz at the end of this lesson. You pass with 60 percent. If an answer is wrong, read the explanation, then reread the part of the lesson it points to.

faqs.q: Do I need to memorise the OSI model?
faqs.a: Not for daily work, but you should know the main layers and where common tools sit: switches at layer 2, routers at layer 3, TCP and UDP at layer 4, HTTP and DNS at layer 7. Interviews often ask.

faqs.q: Why are private IP addresses needed?
faqs.a: There are not enough IPv4 addresses for every device. Private ranges can be reused inside many separate networks, and NAT lets those devices reach the internet through a public address.

faqs.q: Is IPv6 replacing IPv4?
faqs.a: IPv6 adoption keeps growing, and many networks use both. IPv4 is still widespread, so you must understand it, and you should learn IPv6 basics too.

options: The DNS name of a server

lessons.title: Subnetting and CIDR Notation Made Simple
lessons.description: Learn what a subnet mask is, read CIDR notation like /24 and /16, count usable addresses, split a network into subnets and check it with Python.

content.text: When you build a cloud network, the first thing it asks is a range such as 10.0.0.0/16, and then a range for each subnet inside it. People find subnetting scary because of the binary maths in old textbooks. You can do the practical part with one idea and one small table, and you can check every answer with a short Python script. By the end of this lesson you will be able to read /24, size a network and split it into parts.
Why do we need it?

Every cloud network starts with address ranges. If you choose them badly, networks cannot be joined later, or you run out of addresses. Subnetting lets you separate public and private parts and apply different rules to each.
A real-life example

Imagine a block of flats with 256 doors numbered 0 to 255. You decide to give floors of 64 doors to different groups: floor one for offices, floor two for shops. That is subnetting: one big range split into smaller labelled parts.
What a subnet is

A subnet is a smaller network cut from a bigger one. Splitting a network has real benefits. Traffic stays inside its own part, you can apply different security rules to each part (for example one subnet for public web servers and another for private databases), and addresses are organised. In AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, this is exactly how you separate public and private resources.
The subnet mask and CIDR
An IPv4 address has 32 bits. Part of it identifies the network and the rest identifies the device inside that network. The subnet mask tells you where the split is. You will see it written two ways.

items: As a dotted mask: `255.255.255.0`.
As CIDR notation (Classless Inter-Domain Routing): a slash and a number, `/24`. The number is how many bits belong to the network.

content.text: So `192.168.1.0/24` means: the first 24 bits (the first three numbers) are the network, and the last 8 bits are for devices. 8 bits give 2 to the power of 8 = 256 addresses. The more bits for the network, the fewer for devices, so a bigger slash number means a smaller network.
The one table you need

items: **/16** = 65,536 addresses. Mask 255.255.0.0. A common size for a whole cloud network.
**/24** = 256 addresses. Mask 255.255.255.0. A common size for a subnet.
**/25** = 128 addresses.
**/26** = 64 addresses.
**/27** = 32 addresses.
**/28** = 16 addresses.
**/30** = 4 addresses, used for links between two devices.
**/32** = 1 address, a single host.

content.text: The pattern: each time the slash number goes up by one, the number of addresses halves. The size is always 2 to the power of (32 minus the slash number).
Usable hosts

In a normal network, the first address is the network address (the name of the network itself) and the last is the broadcast address (to talk to everyone). Neither can be given to a device. So usable hosts equal total addresses minus 2. A /24 gives 254 usable addresses. Cloud providers reserve a few more in each subnet for their own use, which means a /24 subnet in AWS gives fewer than 254. Always check your provider’s documentation before you size a subnet tightly.
Check it with Python

Python has the `ipaddress` module in its standard library, which does the maths for you. This small script prints the details of any network and splits it into smaller ones. The script in this lesson was run on Linux in the course lab (bash 5, Python 3.13). The output shown is real. Your numbers (memory, disk, dates) will be different.

"""subnet.py - answer the usual CIDR questions with Python's standard library."""
import ipaddress, sys

net = ipaddress.ip_network(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "10.0.0.0/24")
print(f"Network:      {net.network_address}/{net.prefixlen}")
print(f"Netmask:      {net.netmask}")
print(f"Broadcast:    {net.broadcast_address}")
hosts = list(net.hosts())
print(f"Addresses:    {net.num_addresses}")
print(f"Usable hosts: {len(hosts)}  ({hosts[0]} to {hosts[-1]})" if hosts else "Usable hosts: 0")
print(f"Private:      {net.is_private}")

if net.prefixlen < 30:
    new_prefix = min(net.prefixlen + 2, 30)
    print(f"\nSplit into /{new_prefix} subnets:")
    for s in net.subnets(new_prefix=new_prefix):
        print(f"  {s}")
Splitting a network on paper

Say you have 10.0.0.0/24 and need four equal subnets. Four is 2 squared, so you add two bits to the network part: /24 becomes /26. Each /26 has 64 addresses, so the subnets start at 0, 64, 128 and 192: 10.0.0.0/26, 10.0.0.64/26, 10.0.0.128/26 and 10.0.0.192/26. That matches the output above. To check that an address belongs to a subnet, see whether it lies between the first and last address of the range.
Planning a cloud network

items: Choose a private range for the whole network that does not overlap other networks you may join later, for example 10.0.0.0/16. Overlaps make it impossible to connect two networks.
Split it into subnets by role: public, private application, and private database. Make one set in each availability zone.
Give each subnet enough room to grow, but do not waste the whole range. A /24 or /20 is a common choice for a subnet.
Write the plan in a table before you create anything.

content.text: Subnetting tests in interviews are often about simple cases like these. Practise by splitting a /24 into /26 and /27 subnets by hand, then check with the script.
Architecture diagram
Here is the idea as a simple picture. You can use the same diagram in your own notes.

flowchart TD
  VPC[10.0.0.0/16 whole network] --> A[10.0.1.0/24 public subnet]
  VPC --> B[10.0.2.0/24 private app subnet]
  VPC --> C[10.0.3.0/24 private database subnet]
How to check it worked

items: You can say how many addresses a /26 has without a calculator.
You can explain why usable hosts are two fewer than the total.
Your four subnet ranges do not overlap.

content.text: How companies use it

Cloud engineers split a /16 network into /24 subnets for web, application and database tiers in each availability zone. Firewalls and routes are applied per subnet. Overlapping ranges are a common cause of failed VPN and peering projects.
Common errors and how to fix them

items: **Ran out of addresses.** The subnet was too small. Resize or add subnets, and remember providers reserve a few addresses.
**Overlapping ranges.** Choose non-overlapping ranges for every network you may connect.
**Wrong mask in a config.** Check the slash number matches the plan.
**Counting usable hosts wrongly.** Subtract the network and broadcast addresses, and the provider reserved ones.

content.text: Best practices

items: Plan ranges on paper first.
Leave room to grow.
Do not reuse ranges across networks that may connect.
Use /24 or larger subnets for most tiers.
Verify with a tool like the Python script.

content.text: Interview questions with simple answers

items: **What is a subnet?** A smaller network carved out of a larger one.
**What does /24 mean?** The first 24 bits are the network, leaving 8 bits (256 addresses) for hosts.
**How many hosts in a /26?** 64 addresses, 62 usable.
**Why subtract 2?** The network and broadcast addresses are not given to devices.
**What is CIDR?** Notation that writes a network as address plus slash number.
**Why do cloud providers reserve addresses?** For their own services such as the router and DNS.
**How to split a /24 into four?** Make four /26 subnets.
**Why avoid overlapping ranges?** Two overlapping networks cannot be joined.
**What is the netmask for /16?** 255.255.0.0.

content.text: Practical exercises
Try each one yourself before you look at the hint. Struggling for a few minutes is how the skill sticks.

items: Run the script on 172.16.0.0/20 and write down the usable hosts. Hint: `python3 subnet.py 172.16.0.0/20`.
Plan a /16 with two /24 subnets in each of two zones. Hint: Four /24 blocks that do not overlap.
Predict the number of addresses in /27, then check. Hint: 2 to the power of 5.
Which of 10.0.1.5 and 10.0.2.5 is inside 10.0.1.0/24? Hint: Look at the third number.
Split 192.168.10.0/24 into /28 subnets and count them. Hint: 16 subnets.

Make an address plan table for a small company with offices in two cities and a cloud network. No ranges may overlap. Check every range with the script.

Adding two bits to the network part makes it /26. The first subnet holds 64 addresses, from 10.0.0.0.
The next subnet starts 64 higher, at 10.0.0.64.
The last two start at 10.0.0.128 and 10.0.0.192. Together the four use the whole /24.

faqs.q: What does /24 mean?
faqs.a: The first 24 of the 32 bits of the address identify the network. The remaining 8 bits are for devices, which gives 256 addresses.

faqs.q: Why do cloud subnets have fewer usable addresses?
faqs.a: Providers reserve a few addresses in every subnet for their own services such as the router and DNS. The exact number depends on the provider, so check its documentation.

faqs.q: Do I need to do subnetting in binary?
faqs.a: Understanding binary helps, but for daily DevOps work the table of sizes and a tool such as Python’s ipaddress module are enough.

lessons.title: DNS, DHCP, HTTP and HTTPS, TCP and UDP, and Ports
lessons.metaTitle: DNS, DHCP, HTTP, TCP, UDP and Ports
lessons.description: Learn what DNS and DHCP do, how HTTP and HTTPS requests and status codes work, TCP versus UDP, and the common ports a DevOps engineer should know.

content.text: In the last two lessons you learned addresses and networks. Now come the services that make a network usable for people: DNS turns names into addresses, DHCP hands out addresses automatically, HTTP and HTTPS carry web pages, and TCP, UDP and ports decide which program on a machine receives which data. Each one shows up in daily DevOps work, especially when something fails and you must find out why.
Why do we need it?

People use names, computers use numbers. DNS and DHCP make networks easy to use, HTTP carries the web, and ports let many programs share one machine. Most real outages show up as a DNS, port or HTTP status problem.
A real-life example

DNS is the phone book: you look up a name and get a number. DHCP is a hotel reception that hands you a room number when you arrive. A port is a door number inside the building, so the pizza arrives at the right flat.
DNS: the phone book of the internet

People remember names such as example.com. Computers use IP addresses. DNS (Domain Name System) translates one into the other. When you ask for a name, your computer asks a resolver, usually run by your internet provider or a public service. The resolver asks the system of servers that hold the answer, and keeps the reply for a time (the TTL, time to live) so it does not have to ask again. The records you will meet most often are these.

items: **A:** a name to an IPv4 address. **AAAA:** a name to an IPv6 address.
**CNAME:** a name that is an alias of another name.
**MX:** which servers receive email for the domain.
**TXT:** free text, used for domain verification and email security settings.
**NS:** which servers are in charge of the domain.

content.text: When you change a DNS record, old answers stay in caches until the TTL runs out, so changes can take minutes or hours to be seen everywhere. That is called propagation, and it is a common reason for the answer: I changed it, but I still see the old site. Before a planned move, lower the TTL a day ahead. Tools such as `dig example.com` and `nslookup example.com` show what DNS answers. They are not installed in every container image, so you may need to install them.
DHCP: addresses on request

When your phone joins Wi-Fi, nobody types an address in. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) on the router gives the device an address, the subnet mask, the gateway (the way out to other networks) and the DNS server, for a limited time called a lease. Servers usually need a fixed address instead, so they get a static address or a reservation, and cloud providers handle this for you. If a device shows an address starting with 169.254, it did not get an answer from a DHCP server.
HTTP and HTTPS

HTTP is the language of the web. The client sends a request with a method, a path and headers, and the server sends back a status code, headers and a body. HTTPS is the same conversation inside TLS, which encrypts it and proves the server’s identity with a certificate.

items: **Methods:** `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PUT` or `PATCH` changes, `DELETE` removes.
**2xx** success: `200 OK`, `201 Created`.
**3xx** redirect: `301` moved for good, `302` moved for now.
**4xx** the client did something wrong: `400` bad request, `401` not logged in, `403` not allowed, `404` not found, `429` too many requests.
**5xx** the server failed: `500` internal error, `502` bad gateway, `503` unavailable, `504` gateway timeout.

content.text: In DevOps you will see 502, 503 and 504 often. They usually mean a proxy or load balancer could not get a good answer from the application behind it: the app is down, overloaded or slow. Try `curl -I https://example.com` to see the status line and headers, and `curl -v` for the full conversation.
TCP and UDP

items: **TCP** sets up a connection first (the three-way handshake), numbers every piece of data, resends lost pieces and delivers in order. It is reliable and a little slower. Web, email, SSH and databases use it.
**UDP** just sends. There is no connection and no resend. It is fast and light, and fine when old data is useless anyway: video calls, games, DNS lookups.

content.text: Ports

An IP address finds the machine. A port number finds the program on that machine, so one server can run a web server and a database at the same time. Ports go from 0 to 65535. A program listens on a port, and a client connects to it. These are the ones worth knowing by heart.

items: **25 / 587** email sending (SMTP)
**80** HTTP and **443** HTTPS
**3306** MySQL, **5432** PostgreSQL, **27017** MongoDB, **6379** Redis
**3000, 5000, 8080** common for development web apps

content.text: To see what is listening on a Linux machine, use `ss -tlnp` (or `netstat -tlnp` on older systems), which shows the open TCP ports and the program for each. If your app says address already in use, another program holds the port. To test whether you can reach a port from another machine, use `curl` for web services, or the check in the health script of the Linux course.

A service that listens on 127.0.0.1 can only be reached from the same machine. To accept connections from outside, it must listen on 0.0.0.0 (all addresses) or a specific address, and the firewall must allow the port. Mixing these up is the cause of many connection refused problems when a deployment is first set up.
Architecture diagram
Here is the idea as a simple picture. You can use the same diagram in your own notes.

sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant D as DNS
  participant S as Web server
  B->>D: Address of example.com?
  D-->>B: 203.0.113.10
  B->>S: TCP connect on port 443
  B->>S: GET /
  S-->>B: 200 OK and the page
How to check it worked

items: You can explain what a 502 and a 404 mean and who is at fault in each case.
You can say why a DNS change is not seen at once.
You can match each of the ports above to its service.

content.text: How companies use it
Teams manage DNS records for domains, load balancers and email, and use TTLs when moving a service. They read HTTP status codes in monitoring and logs, and check ports when services cannot connect.
Common errors and how to fix them

items: **I changed DNS but still see the old site.** Caching. Wait for the TTL or flush local caches, and lower the TTL before planned changes.
**502 Bad Gateway.** The proxy could not get a good answer from the app. Check that the app is running and healthy.
**504 Gateway Timeout.** The app answered too slowly. Check load, database and timeouts.
**Address already in use.** Another program holds the port. Find it with `ss -tlnp`.
**Service reachable locally but not from outside.** It listens on 127.0.0.1 or a firewall blocks the port.

content.text: Best practices

items: Lower TTL before moves.
Use health endpoints returning 200.
Do not expose databases to the internet.
Use HTTPS everywhere.
Know the common ports.

content.text: Interview questions with simple answers

items: **What does DNS do?** Translates names to IP addresses.
**What is a CNAME?** An alias from one name to another.
**What is TTL?** How long an answer may be cached.
**What does DHCP do?** Gives devices addresses and settings automatically.
**GET vs POST?** GET reads data. POST sends data to create something.
**What does 404 mean?** The page was not found.
**What does 502 mean?** Bad gateway: the proxy got a bad answer from the app behind it.
**TCP vs UDP?** TCP is reliable and ordered. UDP is fast with no guarantee.
**Which port is SSH?** 22.
**What is a port?** A number that identifies a program on a machine.

faqs.q: Why do I still see the old site after I changed DNS?
faqs.a: DNS answers are cached until their TTL expires, on resolvers and sometimes on your own computer or browser. Wait for the TTL, or lower the TTL before the change next time.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 502 and 504?
faqs.a: A 502 means the proxy got a bad answer from the application behind it. A 504 means the proxy waited and got no answer in time. Both point to a problem behind the proxy.

faqs.q: Why is DNS usually UDP and not TCP?
faqs.a: DNS questions and answers are small, so a fast UDP message is enough. DNS falls back to TCP for large answers.

lessons.title: Firewalls, NAT, VPN, Load Balancers, TLS and Network Troubleshooting
lessons.metaTitle: Firewalls, NAT, VPN, Load Balancers, TLS
lessons.description: Understand firewalls and ufw, NAT, VPNs, load balancers, reverse proxies, TLS certificates and CDNs, then follow a simple network troubleshooting method.

content.text: This lesson joins the pieces that sit between a visitor and your application: the firewall that decides what may pass, NAT that lets private machines reach the internet, VPNs that connect networks safely, load balancers and reverse proxies that share the work, TLS that encrypts it, and the CDN that puts copies near the visitor. Then it ends with a simple method for finding network problems. Every cloud lesson later uses these ideas under different names.
Why do we need it?
Between your users and your app sit many network parts that protect it and share the work. If you do not understand them, you cannot secure a service or find why traffic is blocked.
A real-life example

Think of a stadium. Security guards check tickets at the gate (firewall). The ticket office hides the real seat numbers and sells tickets through one window (NAT). Staff guide people to the least crowded entrance (load balancer). A tunnel for players only (VPN). The CDN is like selling snacks at stands near every seat instead of one kitchen.
Firewalls

A firewall allows or blocks traffic using rules. A rule usually names a direction (in or out), a protocol, a port and a source or destination address. The safest approach is to block everything by default and open only what you need. On Ubuntu, the simple tool is `ufw`.

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp        # SSH: allow this BEFORE you enable the firewall
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose

The Red Hat family uses `firewalld` with `firewall-cmd`, and underneath both are built on the kernel feature called nftables or iptables. Cloud providers add their own firewalls at the network edge, called security groups and network ACLs in AWS. A request must pass every firewall on its path, so if a port is open in `ufw` but blocked in the cloud security group, it is still blocked. Always check both. This commands block was not run for this course. Be very careful with remote servers: if you enable a firewall without allowing SSH first, you lock yourself out.
NAT

NAT (Network Address Translation) lets many devices with private addresses share one public address. When a private machine opens a connection to the internet, the NAT device swaps the private source address for its own public one, remembers the conversation, and swaps back when the answer returns. Outside machines cannot start a connection to the private machine, which is a handy side effect. In the cloud, a NAT gateway gives private servers a way out (for updates, for example) without giving them a public address.
VPN

A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates an encrypted tunnel across the internet. A site-to-site VPN joins two networks, for example an office and a cloud network, so they behave like one network. A remote-access VPN lets one person connect to a private network from home. Tools you will meet include WireGuard and OpenVPN, and every big cloud has managed VPN services. A VPN protects the traffic in the tunnel. It does not make a weak server safe.
Load balancers and reverse proxies

items: A **reverse proxy** sits in front of one or more servers and forwards requests to them. Nginx is the common example. It can serve static files, terminate TLS, compress, cache and hide the real servers.

A **load balancer** spreads requests over several copies of an application, and stops sending to a copy that fails its health check. Common ways to pick a server are round robin (take turns) and least connections.
**Layer 4** balancers work with addresses and ports only. **Layer 7** balancers read the HTTP request and can route by path or host name, for example /api to one group and /blog to another.

content.text: A load balancer is what makes a web service both scalable (add more copies) and available (a failed copy is skipped). It needs a health check endpoint in your app, such as /health, that answers 200 only when the app is truly working. The health check script from the Bash lesson is a tiny version of what a load balancer does every few seconds.
TLS and certificates

TLS encrypts the connection and proves who the server is. A certificate says: this public key belongs to this domain, signed by an authority your browser trusts. Certificates expire, and an expired one gives every visitor a scary warning, so renewal must be automatic. Let’s Encrypt is a free authority that issues certificates through the ACME protocol, and tools like Certbot automate it. Cloud providers offer managed certificates that renew by themselves. You can look at a server’s certificate with `openssl s_client -connect example.com:443` or with `curl -vI https://example.com`, and the expiry date is in the output.
Routing, switching and CDN

items: A **switch** connects devices inside one network. A **router** connects different networks and decides the next hop for each packet using a routing table. The default route (0.0.0.0/0) means: for anything I do not know, send it this way, normally to the internet gateway.

A **CDN** (content delivery network) keeps copies of your files on servers in many places, so visitors get them from a nearby server. This makes pages load faster, takes load off your server and can absorb some attacks. It works best for images, scripts and pages that do not change per user.

content.text: Network configuration on Linux

Before you can troubleshoot, you need to see how a Linux machine is set up. These commands only read information, so they are safe to try. They were not run for this course on a real server, and the output differs on every machine.

ip addr                    # interfaces and their IP addresses (older systems: ifconfig)
ip route                   # the routing table, including the default gateway
hostname -I                # just the addresses
cat /etc/resolv.conf       # which DNS servers this machine asks
cat /etc/hosts             # fixed name-to-address entries, checked before DNS
hostnamectl                # the machine name

To make a static address permanent you edit the network configuration of your distribution: Ubuntu uses Netplan files in `/etc/netplan/`, Red Hat style systems use NetworkManager (`nmcli`). In the cloud you almost never edit this by hand, because the provider’s DHCP gives the machine its address, so change addresses in the cloud console or in code instead. A wrong network change on a remote server can cut your own connection, so keep a second way in, such as the provider’s console.
A troubleshooting method
When something cannot connect, do not guess. Go from the bottom up and from near to far, and change only one thing at a time.

items: **Is the name right?** Check DNS with `dig` or `nslookup`.
**Can I reach the machine?** Try `ping` (some networks block it, so a failed ping is not proof).
**Is the port open?** Test from the client with the health script, `curl` or `nc -vz host port`.
**Is the service listening?** On the server, `ss -tlnp` shows what listens and on which address.
**Is a firewall in the way?** Check the local firewall, the cloud security group and any network ACL.
**Does the application answer?** Use `curl -v` and read the status code. Then read the application logs.

content.text: This small script is the port and URL test from the Bash lesson. It tells you at once whether the failure is at the port (nothing is listening or a firewall drops it) or in the application (a status code other than 200). It was run in the course lab against a local test server. The script in this lesson was run on Linux in the course lab (bash 5, Python 3.13). The output shown is real. Your numbers (memory, disk, dates) will be different.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# healthcheck.sh - is a TCP port open, and does a URL answer 200? Exit code 0 = healthy.
# Usage: ./healthcheck.sh <host> <port> [path]
set -uo pipefail
HOST="${1:?host}"; PORT="${2:?port}"; PATH_="${3:-/}"

if ! (exec 3<>"/dev/tcp/$HOST/$PORT") 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "FAIL: $HOST:$PORT is not accepting connections"; exit 1
fi
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -m 3 -w '%{http_code}' "http://$HOST:$PORT$PATH_" || true)
if [ "$CODE" = "200" ]; then
  echo "OK: $HOST:$PORT$PATH_ answered 200"; exit 0
fi
echo "FAIL: $HOST:$PORT$PATH_ answered ${CODE:-nothing}"; exit 1

$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765 /
OK: 127.0.0.1:8765/ answered 200
$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765 /missing
FAIL: 127.0.0.1:8765/missing answered 404
$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765
FAIL: 127.0.0.1:8765 is not accepting connections
Architecture diagram
Here is the idea as a simple picture. You can use the same diagram in your own notes.

flowchart LR
  U((Users)) --> CDN[CDN]
  CDN --> FW[Firewall]
  FW --> LB[Load balancer]
  LB --> A1[App copy 1]
  LB --> A2[App copy 2]
  A1 --> DB[(Database in private subnet)]
  A2 --> DB
How to check it worked

items: You can explain what NAT does and why a private server cannot be reached from the internet directly.
You can say the difference between a reverse proxy and a load balancer.
Your health check shows the three different results when you test OK, 404 and a stopped server.

content.text: How companies use it

Production systems sit behind a load balancer with HTTPS, private application servers, a NAT gateway for outbound traffic and strict firewall rules. Engineers use VPNs for admin access and CDNs for speed and protection.
Common errors and how to fix them

items: **Locked out after enabling ufw.** Allow SSH before enabling. Use the provider console to recover.
**Port open locally but blocked from outside.** Check the cloud security group and network ACL too.
**Certificate expired.** Set up automatic renewal and an expiry alert.
**Load balancer marks all targets unhealthy.** The health check path or port is wrong, or the app is down.
**Cannot reach the internet from a private server.** Add a NAT gateway and a route to it.

content.text: Best practices

items: Deny by default and open only needed ports.
Automate certificate renewal.
Put databases in private subnets.
Use health checks that test the real app.
Log and monitor blocked traffic.

content.text: Interview questions with simple answers

items: **What is a firewall?** A set of rules that allows or blocks traffic.
**What is NAT?** Lets private addresses share a public address by translating them.
**What is a VPN?** An encrypted tunnel across the internet joining devices or networks.
**Reverse proxy vs load balancer?** A reverse proxy forwards to servers. A load balancer spreads traffic and checks health.
**Layer 4 vs layer 7 balancing?** Layer 4 uses addresses and ports. Layer 7 reads the HTTP request.
**What does TLS do?** Encrypts the connection and proves who the server is.
**What is Let’s Encrypt?** A free certificate authority with automatic issuing.
**What is a CDN?** A network of servers that caches content near users.
**How do you troubleshoot a connection?** Name, reachability, port, listening service, firewalls, application.
**Why can a failed ping be misleading?** Many systems block ping on purpose.

content.text: Warning: Changing firewall rules on a remote server can lock you out. The `ufw` commands here were not run on a live server for this course. Test on a practice machine and keep a second way in.
Practical exercises
Try each one yourself before you look at the hint. Struggling for a few minutes is how the skill sticks.

items: Test a local web server with the health script, then stop it and test again. Hint: `python3 -m http.server`.
Check the expiry date of a site certificate. Hint: `curl -vI` or `openssl s_client`.
Draw a request path through CDN, firewall and load balancer. Hint: Use the diagram.
Write a ufw plan that allows only SSH, HTTP and HTTPS. Hint: Default deny incoming.
Explain NAT to a friend with the stadium example. Hint: One window sells to many.

content.text: Mini project: Secure small web server
On a practice Ubuntu machine, install nginx, allow only ports 22, 80 and 443 with ufw, and test each rule from another machine. Record the commands and what you saw.
Knowledge test
Answer the ten questions in the quiz at the end of this lesson. You pass with 60 percent. If an answer is wrong, read the explanation, then reread the part of the lesson it points to.

steps.say: A visitor requests your site over HTTPS.
A CDN may answer from a nearby copy. Firewall rules decide what traffic is allowed through.
The load balancer picks a healthy copy of the application, and skips any that fail the health check.
The application servers live in a private network and answer through the load balancer.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a firewall and a security group?
faqs.a: A security group is a firewall that the cloud provider applies to your virtual machines. The idea is the same: rules about allowed traffic. In AWS, security groups remember connections, while network ACLs do not.

faqs.q: Can a failed ping prove a server is down?
faqs.a: No. Many networks and servers block ping on purpose. Test the real service on its real port instead.

faqs.q: How do I stop certificates from expiring?
faqs.a: Use automatic renewal: Certbot or another ACME client, or a managed certificate from your cloud provider. Add a monitoring alert for the expiry date as a second safety net.

lessons.title: Git for DevOps Teams: Branches, Rebase, Stash, Tags and Pull Requests
lessons.metaTitle: Git for DevOps: Branching and Reviews
lessons.description: Use Git the way DevOps teams do: branching strategies, merge or rebase, stash, reset and revert, cherry-pick, tags for releases, pull requests and code reviews.

content.text: If you already know the basic Git commands, this lesson shows how teams use them to ship software safely. If you are new to Git, first read the free [Git and GitHub course](/learn/git-and-github-course) on this site, then come back, because this lesson assumes you can commit, branch and push. In DevOps, Git is not just where code lives. Pipelines start from it, releases are marked in it, and in GitOps even the live system is described in it. A few habits make that smooth.
Why do we need it?
Every pipeline starts from Git, and teams share one project. Good habits stop people overwriting each other, keep history clean, and make releases and rollbacks easy.
A real-life example

Imagine a team writing one big book. Each writer works on their own copy of a chapter, then the editor merges the chapters. If two writers changed the same sentence, the editor decides which version stays. Git is the system that tracks all copies, edits and decisions.
Branching strategies
A branching strategy is the team’s agreement about which branches exist and how work flows between them. Three are common.

items: **Trunk-based development:** everyone works in very short branches (a day or two) and merges into `main` often. It relies on good automatic tests and, often, feature flags to hide unfinished work. It suits teams that deploy many times a day.
**GitHub flow:** `main` is always deployable. For every change you create a branch, open a pull request, get a review and tests, merge, and deploy. Simple and very popular.
**Git flow:** long-lived `develop` and `main` branches plus feature, release and hotfix branches. It fits software with scheduled releases and several supported versions, but it has more overhead.

content.text: There is no single best choice. For a small team with a web application, GitHub flow is a good start. Whatever you choose, keep branches short-lived: the longer a branch lives, the harder the merge.
Merge or rebase

Both combine work from two branches. A merge adds a new commit that joins the two histories, and keeps everything as it happened. A rebase replays your commits on top of the latest `main`, which gives a straight line of history that is easier to read. The golden rule of rebase: never rebase commits that other people have already pulled, because you rewrite history and cause trouble for them. A safe pattern is to rebase your own private branch on `main` before you open the pull request, and to merge (or squash) when the pull request is accepted.

git switch -c feature/health-endpoint    # start a branch
git add . && git commit -m "Add /health endpoint"
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main                     # replay my work on the newest main
git push --force-with-lease -u origin feature/health-endpoint
`--force-with-lease` is a safer force push: it refuses if someone else pushed to your branch in the meantime. You need a force push after a rebase, because history changed.
Stash, reset and revert

items: `git stash` puts your unfinished changes on a shelf so you can switch branches with a clean folder. `git stash pop` brings them back, and `git stash list` shows the shelf.

`git restore file` throws away changes to a file that you have not committed. `git reset --soft HEAD~1` undoes the last commit but keeps the changes ready to commit again. `git reset --hard` destroys uncommitted work, so think before you use it.
`git revert <commit>` makes a new commit that undoes an old one. Use revert, not reset, to undo something that is already shared, because it keeps the history honest.

content.text: A quick refresher on the everyday commands

items: `git init` starts a repository and `git clone <url>` copies an existing one.
`git add` stages changes, `git commit -m "message"` records them.
`git fetch` downloads new work without changing your files. `git pull` is fetch plus merge. `git push` uploads your commits.
`git status`, `git log --oneline` and `git diff` show where you are.

content.text: Merge conflicts
A conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines. Git cannot choose, so it stops and marks the file. You will see markers like these:

<<<<<<< HEAD
timeout = 30
=======
timeout = 60
>>>>>>> feature/slow-api

items: Open the file and decide what the final text should be: one side, the other, or a mix.
Delete the three marker lines so only the final text remains.
Run `git add <file>`, then `git commit` (or `git rebase --continue` during a rebase).
Run the tests before you push. A conflict that is fixed wrongly still compiles.

content.text: `git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort` takes you safely back to before you started. Small, short-lived branches are the best cure, because they conflict less.
Cherry-pick

`git cherry-pick <commit>` copies one commit onto the branch you are on. DevOps teams use it when a fix made on `main` must also go onto a release branch, without taking all the other changes. Prefer small, focused commits, because cherry-picking a commit that mixes five things is painful.
Tags and releases

A tag is a fixed name for one commit, normally used to mark a release such as `v1.4.0`. Pipelines can start a release build when a tag is pushed, and rolling back means deploying the previous tag. A common numbering scheme is semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where a patch fixes bugs, a minor adds features without breaking things, and a major may break things.

git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0"
git push origin v1.4.0
git tag --list "v1.*"
Pull requests and code review

A pull request (PR) asks for your branch to be merged and gives others the chance to look first. Good PRs are small, have a clear title and description (what changed and why, and how you tested it) and link to the ticket. Good reviews are kind, specific and quick. Reviewers look for bugs, clarity, security and tests, and they separate must-fix from nice-to-have. Automation helps: the pipeline runs tests on every PR, and branch protection rules on `main` can require a passing pipeline and at least one approval before merging. That is how a review step becomes a safe gate in DevSecOps, not a suggestion.

Never commit passwords, API keys or private keys. Once pushed, a secret is in the history even if you delete the file later, and you must treat it as leaked and replace it. Use a `.gitignore` for files like `.env`, and consider a secret scanner in your pipeline.
Architecture diagram
Here is the idea as a simple picture. You can use the same diagram in your own notes.

gitGraph
  commit id: "start"
  branch feature
  checkout feature
  commit id: "add /health"
  commit id: "tests"
  checkout main
  merge feature
  commit id: "release v1.0" tag: "v1.0"
How to check it worked

items: `git log --oneline --graph` shows the history you expect after the rebase.
You can explain when to use revert and when to use reset.
You can name the strategy your own team or project uses, and why.

content.text: How companies use it

Most companies use a pull request flow with required reviews and passing tests. Releases are marked with tags, and hotfixes are cherry-picked onto release branches. Git history is also the audit trail for GitOps.
Common errors and how to fix them

items: **Merge conflict.** Open the file, choose the final text, remove the markers, `git add` and commit.
**Rejected push (non-fast-forward).** Pull or fetch and rebase first, then push again.
**Committed a secret.** Rotate the secret at once. Deleting the file does not remove it from history.
**Detached HEAD.** Create a branch with `git switch -c name` to keep your work.
**Lost commits after reset.** `git reflog` can find them for a while.

content.text: Best practices

items: Short-lived branches and small pull requests.
Clear commit messages.
Rebase private branches, never shared history.
Protect `main` with required checks.
Tag releases.

content.text: Interview questions with simple answers

items: **Merge vs rebase?** Merge joins histories with a merge commit. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch for a straight history.
**What is a pull request?** A request to merge a branch, with review and checks.
**revert vs reset?** Revert adds a commit that undoes an old one. Reset moves the branch back.
**What is cherry-pick?** Copying one commit onto another branch.
**What is git stash?** Shelving unfinished changes.
**What is a tag?** A fixed name for a commit, often a release.
**What is trunk-based development?** Everyone merges small changes into main often.
**What is Git flow?** A model with develop, release and hotfix branches.
**How do you resolve a conflict?** Edit the file, remove markers, add and commit.
**What is `--force-with-lease`?** A safer force push that stops if someone else pushed.

content.text: Practical exercises
Try each one yourself before you look at the hint. Struggling for a few minutes is how the skill sticks.

items: Make a branch, two commits and rebase it on main. Hint: `git rebase main`.
Create a conflict on purpose and fix it. Hint: Edit the same line on two branches.
Undo a pushed commit with revert. Hint: `git revert hash`.
Tag a version and list tags. Hint: `git tag -a`.
Use stash to switch branches mid-change. Hint: `git stash` and `git stash pop`.

content.text: Mini project: Team workflow rehearsal
With a friend or two accounts, create a repository, protect `main`, make a pull request, review it, and merge. Record the steps and tag a release.
Knowledge test
Answer the ten questions in the quiz at the end of this lesson. You pass with 60 percent. If an answer is wrong, read the explanation, then reread the part of the lesson it points to.

steps.say: You do the work on a short-lived branch.
You open a pull request. Tests run and a teammate reviews it.
After approval, it merges into main, which stays deployable.
A tag marks the release commit, so you can deploy it, and roll back to an earlier tag.

faqs.q: Should I use merge or rebase?
faqs.a: Use rebase to keep your own private branch up to date, and merge or squash-merge when the pull request is accepted. Never rebase commits that others have already pulled.

faqs.q: What is the difference between git revert and git reset?
faqs.a: Revert adds a new commit that undoes an earlier one and is safe on shared branches. Reset moves the branch pointer back and can erase history, so use it only on your own unshared work.

faqs.q: What should I do if I committed a secret?
faqs.a: Treat it as leaked: revoke or rotate the secret straight away, then remove it from the code. Deleting the file in a later commit does not remove it from history.

quiz.q: Which command safely undoes a commit that is already shared?
What is the golden rule of rebase?

lessons.title: GitHub Actions: Your First CI Pipeline
lessons.metaTitle: GitHub Actions: Your First CI Pipeline
lessons.description: Build a CI pipeline with GitHub Actions that tests and builds a Node project on every push and pull request, using a matrix, caching and artifacts.

content.text: GitHub Actions is the automation service built into GitHub. When something happens in your repository, for example a push or a pull request, it starts a virtual machine, checks out your code and runs the steps you describe in a YAML file. It is a very good first CI tool, because it needs no server of your own, and the ideas you learn here (triggers, jobs, steps, secrets, artifacts) carry over to Jenkins, GitLab CI and the others. In this lesson you build a pipeline for a small Node project.
Why do we need it?
Running tests by hand is slow and people forget. A pipeline runs the same checks on every change, so mistakes are caught in minutes. GitHub Actions needs no server of your own.
A real-life example
It is like a robot assistant at a factory gate who inspects every product before it leaves. You write the inspection list once, and the robot follows it every time without getting tired.
The vocabulary

items: **Workflow:** one YAML file in `.github/workflows/`. A repository can have many.
**Trigger (`on`):** the event that starts it, such as `push`, `pull_request`, a schedule or a manual button.
**Job:** a group of steps that runs on one fresh machine (a runner). Jobs run in parallel unless you say one `needs` another.
**Step:** one command (`run`) or one reusable action (`uses`).
**Action:** a ready-made step from the marketplace, for example `actions/checkout`.
**Runner:** the virtual machine, such as `ubuntu-latest`.

content.text: The sample project

The project is tiny on purpose: one function, two tests that use Node’s own test runner, and a build script. It was run in the course lab with Node 22: `npm ci` installed with zero packages, `npm test` passed both tests, and `npm run build` printed build finished. The lock file `package-lock.json` is part of the project, because `npm ci` needs it for repeatable installs.
export const sum = (a, b) => a + b;
The workflow file

Save this as `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. The file was checked by parsing the YAML and reading back its triggers, matrix and steps. It was not executed on GitHub for this course, because that needs a real repository, so the first run on your own repository is your final test.

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [20, 22]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: matrix.node == 22
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/
Reading it line by line

items: `on` starts the workflow for pushes to `main` and for pull requests that target `main`.
`strategy.matrix.node` runs the job twice, once with Node 20 and once with Node 22. A matrix is how you test against several versions without copying the job.
`actions/checkout@v4` downloads your code onto the runner. Without it the machine is empty.
`actions/setup-node@v4` installs Node and, with `cache: npm`, keeps downloaded packages between runs to save time.
`npm ci` installs exactly what the lock file says. It is faster and stricter than `npm install`, and it is what CI should use.
`npm test` and `npm run build` are your checks. If any step exits with a failure code, the job stops and turns red.
`upload-artifact` saves the build output so you can download it or use it in a later job. The `if` limits it to one matrix run.

content.text: Pin actions to a version, as in `@v4`, and review third-party actions before you use them. An action runs with access to your repository, so only use ones from sources you trust. For higher safety, teams pin to a full commit hash.
Make the pipeline matter

items: Push the project and the workflow to a GitHub repository, and open the Actions tab to watch the first run.
Break a test on purpose in a branch, open a pull request and watch the check fail.
In the repository settings, add a branch protection rule on `main` that requires this check to pass before merging. Now the pipeline is a real gate.
Fix the test and see the check turn green.

content.text: Secrets

Pipelines often need passwords or tokens, for example to deploy. Store them in the repository settings under Secrets, and read them in the workflow as `${{ secrets.NAME }}`. GitHub hides their values in logs. Never write them into the YAML file, and give each secret only the access it needs. For deployments to a cloud, a better practice you will meet later is OpenID Connect, which lets the workflow get short-lived access without a stored long-lived key.
Next steps

Later lessons add more to this pipeline: building a Docker image, scanning it for vulnerabilities, deploying to a server or Kubernetes, and sending notifications. The pattern stays the same, only more steps. Start small and add one thing at a time, running it after each addition.
Architecture diagram
Here is the idea as a simple picture. You can use the same diagram in your own notes.

flowchart LR
  P[Push or pull request] --> R[Runner starts]
  R --> C[Checkout code]
  C --> I[npm ci]
  I --> T[npm test]
  T --> B[npm run build]
  B --> U[Upload artifact]
  T -->|fail| X[Red check, merge blocked]
How to check it worked

items: The Actions tab shows a green check for both matrix jobs.
A pull request with a failing test cannot be merged when branch protection is on.
You can say what `npm ci` does differently from `npm install`.

content.text: How companies use it
Teams run tests, linters and builds on every pull request, publish images and deploy from tagged releases. Branch protection blocks merges until checks pass.
Common errors and how to fix them

items: **Workflow does not start.** The file is not in `.github/workflows/` or has YAML errors.
**npm ci fails.** Commit `package-lock.json` and keep it in sync with package.json.
**Secret is empty.** Secrets are not passed to workflows from forks. Check the name and where it is defined.
**Works locally, fails in CI.** Different Node version or missing environment variables.
**YAML indentation errors.** Use two spaces and a YAML linter.

content.text: Best practices

items: Pin action versions.
Cache dependencies.
Keep jobs short.
Store secrets in repository settings.
Require checks before merging.

content.text: Interview questions with simple answers

items: **What is a workflow?** A YAML file that defines automation in a repository.
**What is a runner?** The machine that runs a job.
**Job vs step?** A job runs on a runner and contains steps. A step is one command or action.
**What does `on` do?** Defines the events that trigger the workflow.
**What is a matrix?** Runs a job with several values, such as Node versions.
**What is an artifact?** A file saved from a run.
**How do you use secrets?** Store in settings and read as `secrets.NAME`.
**Why `npm ci`?** Repeatable installs from the lock file.
**What is branch protection?** Rules that require checks and reviews before merging.
**How do you run a workflow manually?** Add `workflow_dispatch`.

lessons.title: Cloud Computing Fundamentals: Public, Private, Hybrid, IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
lessons.description: Understand cloud computing, its benefits, public, private, hybrid and multi-cloud, IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, virtual machines and containers.

content.text: Before cloud computing, a company that wanted a website bought servers, put them in a room, connected cables, installed software and hired people to look after the machines. If the website became popular, the servers ran out of power, and ordering new ones took weeks. If it did not, the servers sat idle and the money was wasted. Cloud computing changes this: you rent computing power, storage and services over the internet from a provider, create them in minutes, and stop paying when you delete them.
Why do we need it?
Buying and running servers takes weeks and money up front. The cloud lets teams create what they need in minutes, pay for what they use and grow or shrink quickly.
A real-life example

Owning servers is like owning a car: you pay for it, insure it, repair it, even when it sits in the garage. Cloud is like using taxis or car sharing: you pay for the trips, and the company looks after the cars.
What cloud computing is

Cloud computing means using computing resources, such as servers, storage, databases, networks and software, that belong to a provider and are delivered over the internet, usually paid for by use. The provider owns and runs the buildings (data centres), the hardware and the basic software. You choose what you want and how much, with a web console, a command line or code.
Benefits

items: **Speed:** a server in minutes instead of weeks.
**Pay for what you use:** no big purchase up front. You pay for the time and the amount, though a badly managed account can still become expensive.
**Scale up and down:** add capacity for a busy day and remove it after.
**Reach:** run your service in many countries without building a data centre in each.
**Managed services:** the provider takes care of patches, backups and hardware for things like databases, so your team spends time on its own product.
**Reliability tools:** copies in several places, if you design for them.

content.text: Cloud is not automatically cheaper or safer. A small steady workload can cost more in the cloud than on a rented server, and a wrong setting can expose data. The benefit comes from using it well. Later lessons show how to control cost and security.
Cloud deployment models

items: **Public cloud:** services are run by a provider such as AWS, Azure or Google Cloud and shared between many customers, with strong separation between them. It is the most common model.
**Private cloud:** the infrastructure is used by one organisation only, in its own data centre or hosted for it. It gives more control, and the organisation carries more of the work and cost.
**Hybrid cloud:** a mix of private systems and public cloud, joined together. A bank may keep sensitive records in its own data centre and use the public cloud for websites.

**Multi-cloud:** using more than one public cloud provider, to avoid depending on one, to use the best service of each, or because of company mergers. It adds complexity, so do not choose it only because it sounds safer.

content.text: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS

The three service models are about how much the provider manages for you. A pizza comparison is popular because it works. Making pizza at home means you do everything. Buying a frozen pizza means someone else made it and you bake it. Ordering a delivery means you only eat.

items: **IaaS, Infrastructure as a Service:** you rent the basic building blocks: virtual machines, disks and networks. You install and manage the operating system and everything above it. Examples: AWS EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine. Most control, most work.

**PaaS, Platform as a Service:** the provider also manages the operating system and runtime. You bring your code and settings. Examples: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service, Google App Engine and Cloud Run. Less control, less work.
**SaaS, Software as a Service:** a finished application that you use through a browser or app: Gmail, Google Docs, Microsoft 365, Slack. You manage only your data and users.

content.text: Between these, you will also hear FaaS, Function as a Service, or serverless functions such as AWS Lambda, where you upload a function and the provider runs it only when something calls it. The name serverless does not mean there are no servers. It means you do not manage them.
Virtualization, virtual machines and containers

Cloud providers run many customers on the same physical machines. They can do this safely because of virtualization: software called a hypervisor divides one physical machine into several virtual machines (VMs). Each VM has its own operating system, memory and disk, and cannot see the others. A VM behaves like a real computer, and takes about a minute to start.

Containers are lighter. Instead of a whole operating system for each one, containers share the host’s kernel and are separated by features of Linux. A container holds your application and what it needs, starts in a second or less, and uses much less memory. You will learn containers in depth in the Docker lessons. In short: a VM virtualizes the hardware, and a container virtualizes the operating system. Many systems use both: containers running inside VMs.
Architecture diagram
Here is the idea as a simple picture. You can use the same diagram in your own notes.

flowchart LR
  A[IaaS: virtual machines] --> B[PaaS: platform for your code]
  B --> C[Functions: run code on demand]
  C --> D[SaaS: finished software]
  A -. more control, more work .-> A
  D -. less control, less work .-> D
How to check it worked

You can say the difference between hybrid and multi-cloud.
You can say how a container differs from a virtual machine in one sentence.

content.text: How companies use it
Companies host websites and apps, store data, run analytics and train models in the cloud. They combine managed services with their own code and often use containers.
Common errors and how to fix them

items: **Unexpected bill.** Set budget alerts and delete unused resources.
**Resource not found.** You are in the wrong region.
**Cannot connect to a VM.** Security group or key pair issue.
**Service quota exceeded.** Request a limit increase.
**Public data leak.** Check storage permissions and turn on blocking of public access.

content.text: Best practices

items: Turn on MFA for the root account.
Set billing alerts first.
Tag resources.
Delete practice resources.
Learn one provider well.

content.text: Interview questions with simple answers

items: **What is cloud computing?** Renting computing resources over the internet and paying for use.
**IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS?** You manage more with IaaS, less with PaaS, nothing but your data with SaaS.
**What is hybrid cloud?** A mix of private systems and public cloud.
**What is multi-cloud?** Using more than one public provider.
**What is virtualization?** Dividing one physical machine into several virtual ones.
**VM vs container?** A VM has its own OS. Containers share the host kernel.
**What is serverless?** Running code without managing servers; the provider scales it.
**What is elasticity?** Automatic growing and shrinking with demand.
**Is cloud always cheaper?** No, it depends on the workload and management.
**What is a hypervisor?** Software that creates and runs virtual machines.

content.text: Warning: Cloud resources can create charges. Before any exercise that creates resources, set a budget alert, use the free tier terms you have read, and delete what you created when you finish.
Practical exercises
Try each one yourself before you look at the hint. Struggling for a few minutes is how the skill sticks.
